title: Build your own
subtitle: room server.
summary: The contract @fzlt/core/presence speaks: lockstep inputs, the 12-byte wire protocol, seats, the lobby, resume and the access check, plus the one-room-one-object pattern and a threat checklist.
lead: We run this in our own games. It isn't a hosted service; here's how to build one like it. `@fzlt/core/presence` and `@fzlt/core/presence/check` are **in-house / experimental**: used in our games, not a supported multiplayer service. Our room server is private, so this guide gives you the contract instead: what presence speaks, the full wire protocol, the pattern we built ours on, and the threat checklist we hold it to. A server that keeps this contract works with presence, and with any page that already speaks it.

items.label: message kinds; clients send 3 of them

items: **Lockstep.** Every peer runs the same fixed-step sim from the same seed, which the room hands out. Only inputs cross the wire. The room never runs the game.

**Inputs per tick.** Each step, presence sends one `INPUT` for frame `f + delay` (default 2: 33 ms at 60 Hz) carrying the player's 32-bit input word. A frame runs only once every seat's input for it is in. A missing input stalls the sim (`net.stalls`); it never guesses.
**The hash check.** Every `hashEvery` frames (default 30) it sends a `HASH` of the sim state. `net.desync` is the first frame whose hashes differed, or -1.

**First write wins.** It keeps the first `INPUT` and the first `HASH` it receives per seat and frame, and counts the rest in `net.dropped`. `LEAVE` sets the seat's bit in `net.lost`; `AWAY` sets it in `net.away` until that seat's `RESUME`, and on any `RESUME` presence resends its own inputs for the frames around the current one.

**Joining.** `join(url, signal, protocols, { retry, lobby })` opens the WebSocket and resolves at `WELCOME` with `{ transport, slot, players, seed, mode }`. Before that, `lobby(start, seat, seated, size)` runs on each `LOBBY`, and the host's `start(seats, mode)` sends `START`. After it, a drop (`1006`, or a server restart: `1011`, `1012`, `1014`) reconnects on its own with `resume.<token>` next to your `protocols` (`retry` tries, from 250 ms and doubling: about 16 s by default); meanwhile your own seat is in `net.away`, and when the tries run out it is in `net.lost`. The token stays in memory, never in a URL. Any other close ends the match. The npm release v0.21.2 handles kinds 1 to 4 only (the lobby and resume came after it): there, a page that wants them handles those kinds itself, and presence counts them in `net.dropped`.

body.text: Binary WebSocket messages of exactly 12 bytes, integers little-endian. Anything else (a text frame, any other size) is a protocol error: close the socket with `1009`.

items: Byte 0, `kind`: one of the eight below.
Byte 1, `slot`: a seat, `0` to `players - 1`. The room overwrites it with the sender's real seat before relaying.
Byte 2, `players`: the number of seats in the match (in `LOBBY`, the room's size; in `START`, the count to start at).
Byte 3, `mode`: the host's `START` byte in `WELCOME`, the seated count in `LOBBY`, else 0.
Bytes 4 to 7, u32: the frame (`INPUT`, `HASH`) or the seed (`WELCOME`).
Bytes 8 to 11, u32: the input word (`INPUT`), the state hash (`HASH`) or the resume token (`WELCOME`).

blocks.heading: 3. The message kinds
blocks.subhead: Clients send only `INPUT`, `HASH` and, the host before the start, `START`. Every other kind comes from the room.

items.title: `INPUT` · 1 · a seat → every other seat
items.body: u32 frame, u32 input word. Relay only after the start, and only the first one per seat and frame: each seat's frames must rise. Stamp byte 1 with the sender's seat.

items.title: `HASH` · 2 · a seat → every other seat
items.body: u32 frame, u32 state hash. The same rules as `INPUT`, counted apart from it.

items.title: `WELCOME` · 3 · room → each seat, at the start
items.body: `slot` is your seat, `players` the match's count, `mode` the host's `START` byte (else 0), then the u32 seed (one per room, the same for everyone) and the u32 resume token (random, never 0, sent only to that seat). Sent again to a seat that resumes.

items.title: `LEAVE` · 4 · room → the others, after the start
items.body: `slot` left for good: a clean close, a kick, or its resume hold ran out. Lockstep then waits on that seat, so the game decides what happens: a bot in its place, or the end of the match.

items.title: `RESUME` · 5 · room → everyone
items.body: `slot` is back in its seat. Every peer resends its own inputs for its last few frames; first write wins drops the repeats.

items.title: `AWAY` · 6 · room → the others
items.body: `slot` dropped and its seat is held for a while: show "reconnecting". Lockstep waits meanwhile.

items.title: `START` · 7 · the host (seat 0) → room, before the start
items.body: Byte 2: start once this many are seated (0: now). Byte 3: any byte the game picks, such as its mode or team layout. Never relayed; a `START` from another seat, or after the start, is ignored.

items.title: `LOBBY` · 8 · room → every waiting seat
items.body: On each join and each leave before the start: `slot` is your seat, `players` the room's size, byte 3 how many are seated. Seat 0 is the host, so only it shows a start key.

blocks.heading: 4. Joining: the handshake and the access check

items:
**The URL.** `GET /room/?players=

` as a WebSocket upgrade: one numbered room per `n`, opened for `p` seats. Refuse an `n` you don't run (404), a request that isn't an upgrade (426) and a `p` outside 1 to your seat cap (400).

**The subprotocols.** The client offers `fizlet-rooms` plus its access token: `invite.<code>`, or `pass.<pass>` and `device.<key>` (16 to 64 base64url characters, made once per device). Answer `fizlet-rooms` in the `101`: a browser that offered subprotocols fails the handshake when the server picks none. Tokens never go in the URL, because URLs land in logs.
**Refused before a socket.** `403` with no valid access or from an origin you don't allow, `429` with `retry-after` over a rate, `409` when the room is already open for a different player count.

**Closed after it.** `4000 room full` (full, or already playing), `1008` over the message rate, `1009` for anything but a 12-byte binary message, `1001` with `room not filled`, `room idle` or `room time is up`.

**The sign-in check.** `POST /invite` with a text body: the code, or the pass and the device key on two lines. A text body keeps it a simple request, with no CORS preflight. Answer `200 {"ok":true,"players":N}`, where `N` is the most seats a room takes so a page offers only sizes that can join, or `403 {"ok":false}`. With passes, add `"pass":true` to every answer and a `why` to a refusal: `pass expired`, `pass revoked`, `pass in use on another device` or `pass not valid`. The check takes no seat. Read the body with a limit.

blocks.heading: 5. The lobby: start before the room is full

body.text: Open the room with the most seats the mode can take (`?players=4`). The first to join is seat 0, the host. Every waiting seat hears `LOBBY` on each join and leave. The host's `START` begins the match once `n` seats are taken (0: now), with the seats taken, renumbered `0` to `k - 1` in seat order; `WELCOME` then says `players = k` and carries the host's mode byte. The game fills the empty places with bots, which every peer simulates the same way from the seed. A room without `START` starts when it is full, so a client should handle both.

blocks.heading: 6. Resume: a dropped seat comes back

body.text: A drop is a close with no clean code (`1006`, or a server restart: `1011`, `1012`, `1014`) or a socket error. Hold the seat for a while (our default: 20 s) and tell the others `AWAY`. A clean close (`1000`, `1001`, no code, `3000` to `4999`) or a kick is a leave: `LEAVE` at once.

To come back, the client opens the same room with one more subprotocol, `resume.<token in hex>`, next to its access token. Answer `WELCOME` (the same seat and token), then `RESUME` for that seat, then the other seats' recent `INPUT`s (we keep the last 64 per seat); the others hear `RESUME`. If the old socket still sits in the seat, close it `4001 resumed` and send no `LEAVE`. A wrong or expired token gets the socket closed `4002 seat gone`: a resume never takes a fresh seat.

blocks.heading: 7. The pattern: one room, one stateful object

items: **A stateless front, then one object per room.** The front checks the origin, the rate and the access token, then hands `/room/<n>` to the one object named for that room: on Cloudflare, a Durable Object; elsewhere, one single-threaded process or actor per room. Every message for a room passes through one place, in order, so seating, the start and first write wins need no locks.
**It seats, seeds and relays.** The room never runs the sim, and reads nothing from an input but its frame.

**Idle costs nothing.** We use WebSocket hibernation, so an idle room holds no running object. What a room must remember across a sleep (the seats, the tokens, held seats, the time of the last relayed message) rides in each socket's attachment, not in storage. A seat that leaves or drops clears its attachment, so a woken room never seats a ghost.
**One alarm per room** for every deadline: the lobby, idle, the room's lifetime and the end of each resume hold.
**Measured locally, through `wrangler dev`:** two Fizlet engines play 600 lockstep frames through one room, byte-identical.

blocks.heading: 8. The threat checklist
blocks.subhead: What we hold our own server to. Each line is a check for yours.

items.title: The gate comes before the room
items.body: Check access before any room object is touched. Store codes hashed (we keep SHA-256 of the trimmed, upper-cased code), never the codes. Ours are 10 to 64 characters.

items.title: Tokens stay out of URLs
items.body: Access codes, passes and resume tokens travel in subprotocols or a POST body. Keep request-URL logging off anyway, and log nothing your code reads from a client.

items.title: Rate limits before storage
items.body: Count access checks and joins per IP before the lookup, refused with `429`, and joins per IP into each room, counted by the room before it accepts a socket. Know whether your counter is per process or global.

items.title: Hard caps in code
items.body: Every cap gets a ceiling that config can lower but never lift: rooms, seats, message rate and burst, message size, the lobby, idle and lifetime timers. Your worst case is rooms × seats × rate messages a second, each relayed to the other seats.

items.title: Nobody speaks for anyone else
items.body: Stamp byte 1 with the sender's seat. Relay only `INPUT` and `HASH`; `WELCOME`, `LEAVE`, `RESUME`, `AWAY` and `LOBBY` come from the room. Take `START` from seat 0 only, before the start.

items.title: First write wins
items.body: Pass on only a seat's first `INPUT`, and first `HASH`, per frame: each seat's frames must rise. presence keeps the first it receives too, so a peer can't split the others' sims.

items.title: Resume tokens are seats
items.body: 32 random bits per seat, drawn at the start, sent only to that seat, offered back as a subprotocol, behind the gate and the join rate. A wrong token is closed `4002` and never takes a fresh seat. Tokens die with the hold or a leave.

items.title: Bounded bodies
items.body: Read request bodies with a limit, chunked or not, and stop reading past it.

items.title: Origins stop browsers only
items.body: An origin allowlist keeps other pages' scripts out. Any other client can send any `Origin`: access is the gate.

items.title: Passes, if you hand out play time
items.body: Sign them (we use HMAC-SHA256 over the payload, checked in constant time), cap their lifetime, lock each to the first devices that use it, and keep a revoke list. With passes required and no signing secret set, refuse every join: never fall back to open.

blocks.heading: What the checklist does not protect

items: Requests are billed before your code runs. Rate limits bound what a client makes you do, not the requests themselves: put billing alerts and your platform's DDoS or WAF rules in front.
An access code is a shared secret. Hand out one per person, so one can be revoked.

A malicious peer can still stall the match (lockstep waits), play its own seat however it likes, and report a false hash, which shows as a desync on the honest peers. It can't move another player, run a frame with two different inputs or send room messages.
Room numbers are guessable: anyone with access can take an open seat.
A held seat stalls the others for the hold. After `LEAVE` they still wait, unless the game puts a bot in the seat.
Matches are not private from the server: it sees every input, and presence trusts it.
A room that sleeps forgets which frames it relayed and its recent inputs. presence's own first write wins still holds, and the peers' resends on `RESUME` carry the inputs.
Read IP addresses for counting only: keep them in memory for a minute's window, never store or log them.

items.q: Can I use your room server?
items.a: No. It runs our games and isn't a hosted service, and its code is private now; its earlier history stays in this repository's git log. This guide is the contract, so a server you write works with presence.

items.q: Does a game need its own server code?
items.a: No. The room seats, seeds and relays. The game runs in every browser, the same on each.
It is what our server and presence speak today. presence is BETA: a minor release may change it, and the CHANGELOG says how.
